items.blurb: A study by the National Museum of Natural Sciences (MNCN-CSIC), the National Research Center on Human Evolution (CENIEH) and the University of Alcalá offers a new explanation for the decline of African megaherbivores. These animals, weighing more than a tonne (2,200 pounds) and today including elephants and hippopotamuses, are known for acting as ecosystem engineers. The results, published in Nature Communications, reveal that their loss of diversity throughout history was not due to their being more vulnerable to extinction, as had previously been proposed, but rather that their decline was driven by particularly low rates of speciation—the emergence of new species.

items.title: Life of M by Rachel Cusk review – is this story of a film star based on Natalie Portman?
items.blurb:
A teasing tale of the friendship between a writer and an actor explores the fallout from fame, and the blurring between pretence and reality

M is a celebrated film actor. A star since childhood, now the face of a major fashion brand, she has been famous all her life. That her career closely resembles Natalie Portman’s has been gleefully seized upon by the press, something Rachel Cusk must surely have anticipated: in the novel, M’s first film has its sex scenes cut at her mother’s insistence, as happened with Portman’s 1994 debut Leon, while her ballerina movie is recognisably Black Swan. M is also, in the words of the nameless and genderless narrator of Life of M, “a good sport”. When the narrator suggests writing M’s autobiography, M likes the idea. “Would you just make it up?” she asks.

A celebrity autobiography is seldom the work of the celebrity herself. And yet any suggestion that the narrator will serve as a kind of ghostwriter to M is dispensed with in a few pages. The pair meet for coffee at a luxury hotel and, after the narrator’s partner falls suddenly and seriously ill, for lunch in a restaurant. The lunch is unsatisfactory, an attempt at intimacy that the narrator acknowledges afterwards to have been a mistake. Though M is determined to live as normal a life as possible (“her personal task is to become real, or rather to acquire some reality”), the narrator is uncomfortably aware of their own falseness with M: “It was as if I was acting, while M came across as authentic and real. It was as if she was the only one good enough at acting to attain reality.” After that the two of them do not see one another again “for a long time”.

items.title: Back on track: can Burnham fix the north’s woeful rail services?
items.blurb:
From a new high-speed line to better intercity links, the PM has a chance to tackle problems he criticised as Manchester mayor

For passenger rail travel, the north of England was the future, once. But since that first train from Darlington to Stockton in 1825, many have felt short-changed. As one angry passenger put it, 200 years later: “What is it about the rail industry which makes them think they can treat passengers in the north as second-class citizens?”

That complaint came from the former mayor of Greater Manchester, who frequently set out a different vision for the train services he would like. Now that Andy Burnham is in No 10, he has the opportunity to win those battles – or perhaps see them a little differently. For now, what unresolved issues could the railway expect to be pursued with greater urgency?

items.title: I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me | Simon Jenkins
items.blurb:
The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules

I plead guilty. I have loved and used the streets of London all my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian. Touch wood, I have done so without accident, blemish or insurance claim. Yet now I find myself perpetually on the wrong side of the law. Regulation has become bureaucratic and chaotic.

When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Many years ago, in the crowded corridor of a Manhattan hotel, I was surprised to find myself standing face-to-face with Imelda Marcos, then the first lady of the Philippines. At that time, she was said to possess 3,000 pairs of shoes.

Ryan Naderi’s second-half strike gave an unconvincing Rangers a narrow 1-0 win in the first leg of their Conference League playoff tie against Czech side Jablonec at Ibrox. Derek McInnes got his first win as Rangers manager at the fifth time of asking with a 5-1 thumping of St Mirren on Sunday but there was regression in the goalless first half which brought boos at the interval whistle.

The Govan side pepped up after the break and Naderi opened the scoring from close range in the 50th minute but in the 78th minute the substitute Cammy Devlin was sent off – minutes after coming off the bench – for a high tackle on Jiri Slama to leave Rangers to see out the game with 10 men.

items.title: Ronaldinho, 46, on mission of love and happiness – and maybe goals – at Serie C’s Ravenna
items.blurb:
Brazilian legend pledges excitement at his unveiling for a comeback that is winning over initially disbelieving fans

It seemed like a joke, a hoax, when at 10pm on 19 June, Ravenna broke the news of Ronaldinho’s signing. The Brazilian, a former Ballon d’Or winner and one of the most recognisable figures in world football, had played his last official match in 2015 for Fluminense; a professional signing in Serie C at 46 years of age seemed unrealistic, to say the least. With football’s attention taken by the World Cup, the game was shocked by this bolt from the blue. For the most part, it remained in disbelief.

There was much discussion, in the city and around the world, about the real value of this operation, and we talked about it too, speaking with the mayor, the fans, and the president of Ravenna, Ignazio Cipriani, scion of the family known globally for Harry’s Bar, who is giving his city much more than a dream.

items.title: "Mumma Is Feeling Tired Today": This Mom of 5-YO Explains Why She Never Hides Her Feelings From Her Daughter
items.blurb: This story is part of “Parenting: What Google Won’t Tell You” — The Better India’s people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can’t always answer. You’ve had a long day. You’re tired, your head is full, and all you want is a few quiet minutes. But the moment you walk through the door, your child is ready with a list: “Mumma, play with me! Let’s draw! Can we go outside?” The instinct may be to say, “I’m fine,” or simply push through the exhaustion because you don’t want your child to see you struggling. But what if saying, “Mumma is tired today. I need a little rest," could actually teach your child something valuable? Parents often feel they need to shield children from difficult emotions. Yet children are usually quick to notice when something feels different — a tired face, a quieter voice, a little less patience. When we name what we are feeling calmly, instead of hiding it or letting it spill over, we give them a chance to understand emotions healthily. You don’t have to hide every difficult emotion. Saying “I’m tired” can teach children what healthy emotional expression looks like. Photograph: ( Instagram/ @parenting_with_shivani ) This is something parenting coach Shivani Tyagi, who shares parenting guidance on Instagram as @parenting_with_shivani , recently illustrated through a simple moment with her daughter. After a seven- to eight-hour car journey, Shivani reached a hotel feeling completely exhausted. Her daughter Ahana, meanwhile, was ready to play. “Mama, let’s go for a walk, let’s play, let’s do painting,” she told her. Instead of pretending she was fine, Shivani simply said, “Ahana, I’m very, very tired and exhausted. I need some time.” A little later, Ahana came and sat beside her, giving her hugs and kisses. For Shivani, the moment was a reminder that children don’t necessarily need parents to hide their emotions. They need to see what healthy emotional expression looks like. Children learn emotional expression by watching us When parents hide every difficult feeling, children can still sense that something is wrong. A tight jaw, a heavy silence, or a sudden change in tone can sometimes leave them wondering: Is Mumma upset? Did I do something? Naming the feeling gives them context. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shivani Tyagi - Parent coach, Nutritionist, NLP practitioner (@parenting_with_shivani) “By naming feelings calmly, we teach three things at once: all emotions are allowed here, feelings can be spoken instead of exploded, and hard moments pass,” says Shivani. So instead of silently withdrawing when exhausted, a parent could say , “Mumma is feeling tired today. I need a few quiet minutes to rest.” The child learns that feeling tired is normal, and that taking a break is a healthy response. Try this three-part approach Shivani suggests keeping it simple: name the feeling, say what you need, and reassure your child. For example: Tired: “Mumma’s body is very tired today. I need some rest, then we’ll play.” Frustrated: “I’m feeling frustrated, so I’m going to take a few deep breaths before we talk.” Overwhelmed: “There’s a lot happening today, and I’m feeling it all at once. Let’s slow down together.” Children learn by watching us. When we pause instead of reacting, we show them that big feelings can be handled calmly. Photograph: ( Knot 9 ) The reassurance is important too, particularly when a child seems concerned. Parents can add, “It’s not because of you. Grown-ups get big feelings too, and I know how to take care of mine.” Let them see the feeling, not carry it Expressing emotions in front of children does not mean sharing every adult problem with them. Financial worries, marital conflicts, or health fears are things children do not need to carry. Similarly, intensely venting at a child can make them feel responsible for comforting their parent. The idea is to show them the manageable, healthy version of an emotion: “I’m worried, so I’m going to take a quiet moment,” rather than making them part of the worry. Sometimes, children don’t need a solution. They just need to understand what’s happening — and know that a little love can help. Photograph: ( Instagram/@parenting_with_shivani ) Over time, these small moments can teach children that emotions are neither scary nor something they need to hide. They can say, “I’m sad.” They can ask for a break. They can seek a hug. And, just like Ahana did, they can learn that sometimes the best response to someone saying, “I’m tired,” is simply to sit beside them and offer a little love.

items.title: This Farmer's Son from Sambhajinagar Cleared CA in One Attempt While Winning National Tennis Medals
items.blurb: Under the first golden rays of the morning sun, a young athlete moves swiftly across a tennis court in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Twenty-two-year-old Om Kakad wipes the sweat from his forehead, glances briefly at the clock, and fires back another serve. The match is still alive, the intensity still high. But even as he focuses on the game before him, his thoughts briefly drift to another opponent waiting at home. A Chartered Accountancy textbook. In a few hours, he will leave the court, head home, and settle into a study routine that often stretches late into the night. For years, this was his reality: athlete by morning, CA aspirant by day and night. “People think you have to choose between passion and profession, but I always believed I could do both,” he tells The Better India. Today, the boy who once rushed from the tennis court to his study desk has emerged as a winner in both arenas, clearing all levels of the Chartered Accountancy course in his first attempt while building an impressive Soft Tennis career that includes national gold medals, three golds at the Maharashtra State Olympic Games and recognition as Maharashtra's own ‘Golden Boy’. At 22, Om has already won national medals and three golds at the Maharashtra State Olympic Games, earning recognition as Maharashtra’s ‘Golden Boy’. His story is not simply about talent. It is about discipline and about a family that believed in him. Most of all, it is about challenging a belief that has long shaped the lives of young Indians — that passion and profession cannot coexist. Refusing to pick just one dream Growing up in a farming family in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Om's earliest ambitions had little to do with balance. He simply loved sports. While academics were always important at home, it was the thrill of competition that excited him. Every tournament became a new challenge, every victory a reason to dream bigger. His father, Ravindra Ramdas Kakad, remembers a young boy who was happiest when he was playing. "He always liked sports," he says. "But we also wanted him to get a good education and become financially independent. We never wanted him to feel that he had to choose one over the other." That support would become crucial in the years ahead. Om's sporting journey truly began in Class 9 when he took up Soft Tennis. The sport was still unfamiliar to many around him, but he quickly showed promise. That same year, he won his first national gold medal. Even today, years and dozens of medals later, he considers that victory one of the most special moments of his life. "It was my first national medal, and I was representing Maharashtra," he recalls. "Winning at that age gave me confidence that I could achieve something big." The win marked the beginning of a journey that would take him across district, state and national competitions. But unlike many young athletes, Om's report card was keeping pace with his medal tally. Om discovered Soft Tennis in Class 9, and within the same year, won his first national gold medal. He scored 95.20 per cent in Class 10 and later secured 88 per cent in Class 12 while studying Science. For most students, those scores would naturally lead towards engineering or medicine. But Om's path took an unexpected turn. The leap from Science to CA After Class 12, he faced a question familiar to countless young athletes: what comes next? Sport remained his first love, but he also knew he needed a profession that would provide long-term stability. The answer came in the form of Chartered Accountancy. "It was a respected course, and it offered nationwide recognition," Om says. "I knew that if I worked hard enough, the result would depend on my effort." The shift was unconventional. Moving from a Science background to Commerce and then entering one of India's most demanding professional courses was never going to be easy. Yet the challenge appealed to him. Looking back, he believes sport had already prepared him for the grind. "When you play competitive sport, you learn how to handle pressure," he says. "That helped me during CA preparation. And CA taught me patience and consistency, which helped me in sports." The years of juggling two demanding worlds If winning medals demanded physical endurance, pursuing Chartered Accountancy demanded a different kind of stamina altogether. For nearly five years, Om's life revolved around a schedule that left little room for leisure. His mornings began before sunrise. By six o'clock, he would already be on the court, training for hours. Once practice ended, the athlete in him had to make way for the student. Om’s parents never asked him to choose between sport and studies. Their belief gave him the freedom to pursue both with equal commitment. "There were days when I studied for 14 to 15 hours," Om says. "When articleship started, I would train in the morning, work in the office from morning till evening and then attend classes at night. It was hectic, but I knew what I wanted to achieve." What made the challenge even harder was that neither of his pursuits allowed shortcuts. Competitive sport demands consistency. Chartered Accountancy demands discipline, and excelling in one often requires sacrifices. Excelling in both requires a level of commitment that can quickly become exhausting. Yet giving up was never something he seriously considered. "It was always a mental game," he says. "People see the medals and the result, but they don't see the sacrifices behind them. Every day was about managing time and staying focused." There were moments when exams approached, and tournaments loomed large. Moments when he wondered whether he should skip a competition and study instead. Moments when training sessions felt impossible after long hours with textbooks. Each time, his family reminded him why he had started. "My parents always supported me," he says. "Whenever I thought about focusing only on studies or only on sports, they encouraged me to continue both. They believed that balancing both would make me different." When one dream strengthened the other Ask Om what helped him survive those years, and he does not point to intelligence or talent. Instead, he talks about pressure. Years of competing at district, state and national tournaments had taught him something that many students struggle with: how to stay calm when everything is on the line. "In sports, pressure is normal," he says. "Every important match comes with pressure. You learn how to deal with it. When I prepared for CA Final, I realised it was the same situation. The pressure was different, but the feeling was the same." That experience proved invaluable in examination halls. Sport taught Om how to handle pressure, while CA taught him patience and consistency. Together, they strengthened the qualities he needed in both. At the same time, the CA journey reshaped him as an athlete. "CA taught me that hard work matters more than talent," he says. "Whenever I felt like giving up in sports, I remembered what CA had taught me. Hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard." In many ways, the two worlds were not competing against each other at all. They were making each other stronger. The day the 'Golden Boy' was born By 2023, Om was deep into his CA journey. His articleship was underway, his schedule was packed and balancing responsibilities had become second nature. Then came the Maharashtra State Olympic Games, popularly known as the Mini Olympics. The event brought together some of the state's finest athletes. Competing in the senior category, Om entered multiple events with little fanfare. He left with three gold medals. "It felt like a comeback," he says. The achievement became one of the defining moments of his sporting career. The following year brought more success when he secured two bronze medals at the 21st Senior National Soft Tennis Championship in Punjab, further strengthening his credentials on the national stage. From early-morning training to late-night study sessions, Om’s mother, Anita, helped him navigate the demanding routine that made both dreams possible. Along the way came recognition in the form of the Samajratna Award for excellence in education and sports, as well as appreciation from Japanese coaches associated with Soft Tennis. But despite the accolades, Om still speaks most fondly about the first national gold medal he won as a school student. "That was where everything started," he says. "That medal made me believe I could achieve something big." The result that changed everything If there was one day that rivalled the joy of standing on a podium, it was result day. Every CA student knows the feeling. When the CA results flashed ‘Successful’, years of early mornings, long study sessions and sacrifices came together in one unforgettable moment. The anxious wait, the website refreshes, and the racing heartbeat, along with hope that years of sacrifice will finally be rewarded. Om remembers staring at the screen as the result page loaded. "The website usually hangs for a few moments," he says, laughing. "When it finally opened, I saw the word 'Successful'." For a few seconds, he could hardly believe it. Then came the realisation. He had done it. "I shouted at home that I had become a CA," he recalls. "Everyone was so happy. There were calls, messages and celebrations throughout the day." Soon came newspaper coverage, felicitations and congratulatory messages from people who had followed his journey. For his family, it felt like the culmination of years of effort and for Om, it was proof that the sacrifices had been worth it. Om's father, Ravindra, still remembers the long days when his son would wake up before dawn for practice and continue studying until late at night. The family's support extended far beyond encouragement. There were long commutes, tournament expenses and countless adjustments to ensure Om could continue pursuing both dreams. His mother, Anita Ravindra Kakad in particular, played a pivotal role in helping manage the demanding routine. Looking back, his father says he never imagined his son would become both a Chartered Accountant and a national-level athlete. With his CA qualification secured, Om is now setting his sights on the international Soft Tennis stage. But once he saw Om's determination, there was no question about supporting him. "When we realised he could do both, we stood behind him completely." Today, he hopes more parents will do the same. "Children should be encouraged to follow their interests," he says. "Sports can also become a career." A dream that is still unfolding For many people, becoming a Chartered Accountant at 22 would be the finish line. For Om, it is only one milestone. His next goal is clear: representing India on the international stage. In a country where young people are often told that success demands choosing one path and abandoning another, Om chose a different route . He carried textbooks and a tennis racquet with equal seriousness. He learnt to live with exhaustion, pressure and uncertainty. And in doing so, he proved that ambition does not always have to fit into a single box. Somewhere today, a student may be wondering whether to give up a sport for studies. Somewhere else, a young athlete may believe that a demanding professional degree is beyond reach. From a young athlete winning his first national gold to becoming a CA at 22, Om’s journey has been shaped by the courage to pursue both dreams. Om's journey offers another possibility. The possibility of showing up before sunrise for training and returning home to study. Of embracing both passion and profession without apologising for either. Of understanding that success is not always about choosing between two dreams. Sometimes, it is about finding the courage to pursue both. As Om puts it, in words that perhaps best capture his journey: "Education is part of life, but your passion is the art of life." And for him, that art is still being perfected — one match, one challenge and one dream at a time. All images courtesy Om Kakad

items.title: I Will Stay Alive For You | Ananya & Soumen ❤️
items.blurb: “And through it all, he never says, ‘I won’t survive.’ He says, ‘I will stay alive for you.’” — Ananya ❤️ Love isn't always about choosing the easiest life. Sometimes, it's about choosing each other when life gets difficult, holding on through uncertainty, and finding hope even when the odds seem impossible.
